enrichment.short_title: Pre-action disclosure of accountant working papers in solicitor negligence claim
key_facts: Former partners of Jay Benning & Peltz retained Wilder Coe to prepare annual accountant's reports for 1996–97 and 1997–98 under the Solicitors Act 1974.

After cashier Mr Belal left in October 1998, successor auditors Munday Long identified a substantial client account shortfall (estimated over £591,000) that had existed by 31 March 1998 but was undetected in the earlier reports.

The applicants contended the accountants negligently failed to verify controls and test client ledger balances; they sought pre-action disclosure of working papers to investigate which accounts were tested.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under CPR 31.16 for pre-action disclosure before contemplated professional negligence proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; order made for disclosure of files and working papers relating to the 1997 and 1998 accountant's reports.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 31.16 conditions were satisfied: the parties were likely to be parties to subsequent proceedings, the documents would fall within standard disclosure, and pre-action disclosure was desirable to resolve or fairly dispose of the dispute; applying Black v Sumitomo Corporation, the court exercised discretion to order disclosure of working papers directly related to allegedly negligent professional work despite some residual speculation about the claim.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 31.16 conditions (a)–(d) were satisfied
Whether pre-action disclosure should be refused as a fishing expedition
Discretionary factors where a professional negligence claim lacks full pleading detail

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on s135 MHA warrant validity and execution.

enrichment.short_title: Section 135 MHA warrant valid but unlawfully executed when named professionals absent
key_facts: Susannah Ward was removed from her home under a section 135 warrant and detained overnight at Sutton Hospital in July 1997.
The warrant identified premises in the information section but left the address blank in the authorisation; it named Dr Forrest, Mrs Carcano-Harley and Dr Thomas to accompany the constable.
PC Welsh executed the warrant accompanied by Mrs Carcano-Harley and Dr Francis (registrar), not the named consultant or GP; Ward was discharged the next day.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Recorder Layton QC's preliminary issue decision in false imprisonment proceedings under section 139 Mental Health Act 1983.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; warrant held valid but execution unlawful because it did not comply with the lawful condition as to named accompanying professionals; matter remitted to Central London County Court.
enrichment.ratio: A magistrate granting a section 135(1) warrant has implicit power to impose conditions on its exercise, including limiting who may accompany the constable under section 135(4); where specific professionals are named on the warrant, execution without them is unlawful even though section 135(4) does not require naming and any ASW and registered medical practitioner would otherwise suffice.
legal_issues: Whether a section 135 warrant with a blank premises field in the direction was invalid
Whether naming accompanying professionals on the warrant creates enforceable conditions
Whether a magistrate may impose conditions including time limits on section 135 warrants
Lawfulness of removal and detention where execution breached warrant conditions

enrichment.short_title: Specific issue orders for childhood immunisation upheld; welfare test not two-stage

statutes_considered.title: United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child

key_facts: Two consolidated cases involved unmarried fathers with parental responsibility seeking specific issue orders under section 8 for full childhood immunisation; mothers were primary carers and strongly opposed.
Sumner J heard extensive expert evidence over 12 days; Dr Conway and Professor Kroll supported immunisation while Dr Donegan's evidence was rejected as unreliable.
The judge ordered immunisation schedules for both children and refused permission to appeal; mothers appealed on alleged misdirection as to the welfare test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted against refusal of permission to appeal from Family Division specific issue order proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted but appeals dismissed; Sumner J's orders for immunisation upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Hotly contested immunisation disputes fall within the small group of important parental decisions requiring court approval; the judge may properly resolve expert medical evidence before conducting a comprehensive welfare survey, provided the paramount consideration under section 1 is ultimately applied — a sequential analysis of medical benefit and non-medical factors is not an erroneous two-stage presumption in favour of vaccination.
legal_issues: Correct legal test for specific issue orders on immunisation
Whether resolving expert evidence first creates an improper presumption in favour of vaccination
Status of immunisation as preventative healthcare versus non-essential invasive treatment
Relevance of primary carer's opposition to court-ordered vaccination

notes: Complete judgment on section 42 leave and IPT jurisdiction.

enrichment.short_title: Vexatious litigant granted leave to continue Investigatory Powers Tribunal claim
key_facts: Mr Ewing was subject to a civil proceedings order under section 42 Supreme Court Act 1981 requiring leave to institute civil proceedings.

He sought retrospective leave to continue an application to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal alleging human rights breaches arising from the Security Service's NCND (neither confirm nor deny) response to his Data Protection Act subject access request.
The Security Service replied that section 28 national security exemption applied and gave no confirmation whether personal data was held.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for leave under section 42(3) to institute or continue civil proceedings before the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted to continue the IPT claim; tribunal held to be a court within section 42 and reasonable grounds for the proceedings established.
enrichment.ratio: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal is a court within section 42 because it exercises judicial functions analogous to High Court judicial review over intelligence services conduct, notwithstanding security-related procedural restrictions; a vexatious litigant need not adduce evidence of specific data held to show reasonable grounds for exercising a statutory right of complaint to the exclusive tribunal where the NCND policy and alleged Convention breaches provide sufficient basis for leave.
legal_issues: Whether the Investigatory Powers Tribunal is a court for section 42 purposes
Construction of section 42 following Attorney General v BBC and Peach Gray
Whether reasonable grounds exist for IPT proceedings by a civil proceedings order subject
Human Rights Act compatibility of restricting access to tribunals

notes: Complete administrative court appeal on magistrates' costs discretion.

enrichment.short_title: Magistrates wrongly refused costs after wrongly applying fresh-application policy to renewals
key_facts: Leigh Powell applied to Swansea City Council to renew and transfer four hackney carriage vehicle licences before expiry on 31 March 2002.

The council returned applications in May 2002 citing missing transfer evidence and home address, then refused renewal in July 2002 for failure to comply with policies applicable to fresh applications.
Swansea justices allowed Powell's appeal, finding applications were timely and correctly completed, but refused his costs relying on Bradford v Booth.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' court on refusal of costs after successful hackney carriage licence renewal appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Stated case answered yes; magistrates erred in law in refusing costs; case remitted for assessment of sum; £3,000 costs summarily assessed for the High Court hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 64(1) Magistrates' Courts Act 1980 and the Bradford City MDC v Booth principles, costs need not follow the event but should reflect whether the regulatory authority acted honestly, reasonably and on grounds that reasonably appeared sound; where justices found the appellant had complied and the council wrongly applied a fresh-application policy to renewal applications, refusal of costs was inconsistent with those findings and an award was plainly warranted.
legal_issues: Application of Bradford v Booth costs principles to licensing appeals
Whether magistrates erred in refusing costs given their findings on the merits
Distinction between renewal and fresh hackney carriage applications

enrichment.short_title: Claim form service extension upheld where defendant waived jurisdiction challenge
key_facts: The claimant suffered severe traumatic brain injury at Tamworth Leisure Centre on 24 April 1999; claim form issued 23 April 2002, one day before third anniversary but date of knowledge was later due to post-traumatic amnesia of around eleven weeks.
Solicitors obtained without-notice extension to 23 December 2002 for service; claim form served 19 December 2002; Master Leslie set aside extension and service in March 2003.

Defendant insurers engaged with pre-action protocol correspondence from August 2002, requested witness details, encouraged medical expert instruction, and acknowledged service ticking box 1 only (defend, not contest jurisdiction).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with re-hearing from Master's order setting aside without-notice extension of time for service and service of claim form.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; extension and service remain valid; defendant's late application to set aside refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant mistakenly applied under CPR Part 7.6(2) for prospective extension rather than serving and seeking extensions for particulars, setting aside is disproportionate if the defendant suffered no prejudice, was notified of proceedings, and by conduct waived the right to contest jurisdiction; a Master who misapplied limitation expiry and treated late instruction as disentitling relief exercised discretion on a mistaken factual basis.

Whether without-notice Part 7.6(2) extension should be set aside
Waiver of jurisdiction challenge by pre-action conduct and acknowledgement of service

Application of overriding objective to set-aside applications

enrichment.short_title: Letter of credit illegality defence arguable where Enron swaps disguised loan

statutes_considered.title: Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (1993 Revision)

key_facts: Mahonia, a Jersey SPV, demanded US $165 million under a standby letter of credit issued by West LB for Enron/ENAC following Enron's Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
The credit secured circular swaps structured to provide Enron a $350 million disguised loan not recorded as debt in US GAAP accounts, contrary to alleged US securities law.
West LB refused payment despite conforming demand; at presentation it had no knowledge of the alleged illegality.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications to strike out and for summary judgment on illegality/public policy defence to payment under documentary credit.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications dismissed; illegality defence held at least strongly arguable with realistic prospect of success at trial.
enrichment.ratio: Although letters of credit are autonomous from underlying transactions and fraud may be resisted only on clear evidence at presentation, illegality affecting the purpose of the underlying scheme may provide an ex turpi causa defence to enforcement where the credit is integral to an unlawful transaction known to the beneficiary; a bank's lack of knowledge at payment date does not necessarily preclude relying on clear evidence of illegality at trial, analogously to the fraud exception analysed in United City Merchants and Balfour Beatty.
legal_issues: Whether illegality of underlying transaction can defeat letter of credit payment
Application of autonomy principle versus ex turpi causa
Whether clear evidence of illegality at trial suffices if absent at presentation
Distinction between tainted purpose and collateral rights under Bowmakers/Tinsley
Enforceability of contracts with foreign illegal purpose under Regazzoni v Sethia

enrichment.short_title: Rule 33 power to allow asylum appeal without merits not mandatory after HO procedural default
key_facts: Mr Benkaddouri, an Algerian health technician, claimed asylum fearing the GIA and Algerian authorities after being coerced to assist the armed Islamic faction.
The Home Office repeatedly failed to comply with IAA directions over three years, including non-attendance at a hearing and failure to identify the operative refusal letter.
The adjudicator declined to allow the appeal under rule 33(2)(a) without considering merits once the refusal letter was identified; the IAT upheld dismissal on both procedure and merits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to Court of Appeal on construction and exercise of rule 33 Immigration and Asylum (Procedure) Rules 2000; renewed application on merits refused.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on the rule 33 issue; adjudicator's refusal to allow appeal without considering merits upheld; permission to appeal on merits refused.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 33(1) should be read as permitting disposal under rule 33(2) where necessary having regard to the overriding objective; the decision is an exercise of judgment not unfettered discretion, but allowing an appeal without considering merits is not mandatory where procedural failures have not made a fair hearing impossible and the appellant agreed to proceed on an identified refusal decision — asylum is not a default entitlement analogous to acquittal in criminal proceedings.
legal_issues: Construction of rule 33(1) and relationship to overriding objective in rule 30(2)
When adjudicator may allow appeal without considering merits after Home Office procedural breach
Whether merits may be considered at all in deciding to use rule 33(2)(a)
Analogy with criminal proceedings and abuse of process

enrichment.short_title: Tomlin settlement enforced against publisher; knowing interference claim fails
key_facts: A 1996 Tomlin order settled passing off proceedings between BPL and MINL, restricting MINL's use of 'Bargain' and specified get-up features and requiring MINL to procure adherence by parent, subsidiary and associated companies.

Corporate reorganisations left Trinity Mirror plc as MINL's parent and MNL (formerly controlled by MINL) launched 'Bargain Hunter' in January 2003 with similar get-up, prompting fresh passing off proceedings by BPML.
BPL applied in the original action to join parties and enforce the settlement; MINL conceded joinder of BPML but opposed joinder of MNL and Trinity Mirror.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in stayed passing off action for liberty to apply under Tomlin order to join parties and enforce 1996 settlement terms.
enrichment.outcome: BPML joined as claimant; enquiry as to damages ordered against MINL for breach of clause 6.1; application otherwise dismissed — MNL and Trinity Mirror not joined; mandatory injunction refused.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 6.1 of the settlement imposed a continuing obligation on MINL to procure adherence by companies falling within the defined corporate descriptions from time to time; breach in failing to procure Trinity Mirror and former subsidiary MNL sounds in damages but refusal to adhere cannot constitute unlawful interference with contract because the claimant has no right to compel third parties to become parties; a third party's mere refusal to adhere is not active prevention or hindrance within Torquay Hotel v Cousins.

Whether MNL's Bargain Hunter publication breached clause 2.2 get-up restrictions

enrichment.short_title: Wasted costs order set aside where joint venture pleadings remained arguable
key_facts: Mr Dempsey claimed trade secrets and breach of an oral joint venture agreement for 10% commission on the Domineye CCTV home security system developed through companies controlled by Mr Johnstone.

After counsel advised withdrawal of the IP claim in February 2002, the contractual joint venture claim continued; the defendant applied to strike out relying on Patel v Patel, shown on the first day of trial.
HHJ George made a wasted costs order against Dempsey's solicitors for costs from 22 February 2002, finding no reasonably competent solicitor could have pursued the claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against wasted costs order under section 51 Supreme Court Act 1981 following strike-out of remaining contractual claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; wasted costs order set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 51(7) 'negligent' is untechnical and denotes failure to act with ordinary professional competence, but where privilege is not waived a wasted costs order for pursuing a hopeless case requires satisfaction that no reasonably competent adviser could have continued — pleadings asserting an oral joint venture with continuing commission obligations independent of company formation remained capable of supporting the claim as a matter of law, and Patel v Patel was fact-specific authority not establishing an inflexible rule precluding such claims.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'negligent' in section 51(7) wasted costs jurisdiction
Whether pursuing a hopeless case requires abuse of process or something beyond negligence
Effect of Patel v Patel on joint venture claims surviving company formation
Role of privilege and legal aid in wasted costs applications
Causation and abatement for counsel involvement
